claim: The nervous system must adapt to a growing body during postembryonic development.
source: During postembryonic development, the nervous system must adapt to a growing body.
evidence: This is a general statement about developmental biology presented in the abstract.

claim: Cellular neuroanatomy underlying synaptic connectivity in Drosophila was previously measured.
source: Previously , we measured the cellular neuroanatomy underlying synaptic connectivity in Drosophila (Schneider-Mizell et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Neuronal morphology and connectivity change between first instar and third instar larval stages.
source: Here, we examined how neuronal morphology and connectivity change between first instar and third instar larval stages using serial section electron microscopy.
evidence: This is the main research question addressed by the study.

claim: Nociceptive circuits were reconstructed in a larva of each stage.
source: We reconstructed nociceptive circuits in a larva of each stage and found consistent topographically arranged connectivity between identified neurons.
evidence: Describes the experimental approach and findings.

claim: There is consistent topographically arranged connectivity between identified neurons across larval stages.
source: We reconstructed nociceptive circuits in a larva of each stage and found consistent topographically arranged connectivity between identified neurons.
evidence: Main finding from the reconstruction data.

claim: Five-fold increases occur in size, number of terminal dendritic branches, and total number of synaptic inputs between first and third instar.
source: Five-fold increases in each size, number of terminal dendritic branches, and total number of synaptic inputs were accompanied by cell type-specific connectivity changes that preserved the fraction of total synaptic input associated with each pre-synaptic partner.
evidence: Quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: Cell type-specific connectivity changes preserve the fraction of total synaptic input associated with each pre-synaptic partner.
source: Five-fold increases in each size, number of terminal dendritic branches, and total number of synaptic inputs were accompanied by cell type-specific connectivity changes that preserved the fraction of total synaptic input associated with each pre-synaptic partner.
evidence: Main finding about connectivity preservation.

claim: Precise patterns of structural growth act to conserve the computational function of a circuit.
source: We propose that precise patterns of structural growth act to conserve the computational function of a circuit, for example determining the location of a dangerous stimulus.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation of the findings.

claim: Developing neural circuits can produce new behaviors, such as the addition of new swimming strategies in zebrafish.
source: While developing neural circuits can produce new behaviors, such as the addition of new swimming strategies in zebrafish (Björnfors and El Manira, 2016), in many cases circuit function is conserved as an animal grows.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In many cases circuit function is conserved as an animal grows.
source: While developing neural circuits can produce new behaviors, such as the addition of new swimming strategies in zebrafish (Björnfors and El Manira, 2016), in many cases circuit function is conserved as an animal grows.
evidence: General statement about developmental neurobiology.

claim: A Drosophila larva's body wall surface area grows by two orders of magnitude from first instar to third instar.
source: For example, as a Drosophila larva grows from a first instar just out of the egg to a third instar ready to pupariate, its body wall surface area grows by two orders of magnitude (Keshishian et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Mechanosensory neurons grow their dendrites to maintain receptive fields during larval growth.
source: To accommodate this growth, mechanosensory neurons grow their dendrites to maintain receptive fields (Grueber et al., 2002), while larval motor neurons add more synapses at the neuromuscular junction and change firing properties to maintain functional responses in much larger muscles (Keshishian et al., 1993; Guan et al., 1996; Davis and Goodman, 1998; Rasse et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Larval motor neurons add more synapses at the neuromuscular junction during growth.
source: To accommodate this growth, mechanosensory neurons grow their dendrites to maintain receptive fields (Grueber et al., 2002), while larval motor neurons add more synapses at the neuromuscular junction and change firing properties to maintain functional responses in much larger muscles (Keshishian et al., 1993; Guan et al., 1996; Davis and Goodman, 1998; Rasse et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Larval motor neurons change firing properties to maintain functional responses in much larger muscles.
source: To accommodate this growth, mechanosensory neurons grow their dendrites to maintain receptive fields (Grueber et al., 2002), while larval motor neurons add more synapses at the neuromuscular junction and change firing properties to maintain functional responses in much larger muscles (Keshishian et al., 1993; Guan et al., 1996; Davis and Goodman, 1998; Rasse et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Functional maintenance has been observed in cricket mechanosensory interneurons.
source: Similar functional maintenance has been observed in central circuits as well, from the frequency selectivity of cricket mechanosensory interneurons (Murphey and Chiba, 1990) to motor rhythms in crustacean stomatogastric ganglion (STG) (Bucher et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Functional maintenance has been observed in motor rhythms in crustacean stomatogastric ganglion.
source: Similar functional maintenance has been observed in central circuits as well, from the frequency selectivity of cricket mechanosensory interneurons (Murphey and Chiba, 1990) to motor rhythms in crustacean stomatogastric ganglion (STG) (Bucher et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: A neuron's function arises from the combination of its morphology, synaptic connectivity, and ion channel properties.
source: A neuron's function arises from the combination of its morphology, synaptic connectivity, and ion channel properties.
evidence: General principle of neuroscience.

claim: If morphology and membrane properties co-vary in precise ways, a neuron's integration properties can be consistent across homologous cells, even between species with very different brain sizes.
source: If morphology and membrane properties co-vary in precise ways, a neuron's integration properties can be consistent across homologous cells, even between species with very different brain sizes (Cuntz et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Homeostatic regulation of functional and structural properties has been proposed as a key principle in neuronal development.
source: Homeostatic regulation of functional and structural properties has been proposed as a key principle in neuronal development, allowing consistent output in the presence of both growth and an uncertain or ever-changing environment (Kämper and Murphey, 1994; Bucher et al., 2005; Marder and Goaillard, 2006; Tripodi et al., 2008; Giachello and Baines, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Simulations of STG have found that numerous different combinations of intrinsic functional parameters and synaptic weights are able to produce extremely similar dynamics.
source: Simulations of STG have found that numerous different combinations of intrinsic functional parameters and synaptic weights are able to produce extremely similar dynamics (Grashow et al., 2010; O'Leary et al., 2014; Prinz et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The morphological structure of neurons and their functional connection strengths have been observed to have high inter-animal variability while still generating similar motor patterns.
source: Correspondingly, the morphological structure of neurons (Otopalik et al., 2017) and their functional connection strengths (Goaillard et al., 2009) have been observed to have high inter-animal variability while still generating similar motor patterns.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Synaptic-resolution electron microscopy reconstructions from Drosophila sensory systems have found relatively low intra-animal variation in number of synaptic contacts between columnarly repeated neurons in the adult visual system.
source: However, synaptic-resolution electron microscopy (EM) reconstructions from Drosophila sensory systems have found relatively low intra-animal variation in number of synaptic contacts between columnarly repeated neurons in the adult visual system (Takemura et al., 2015) or bilaterally repeated neurons in the mechanosensatory (Ohyama et al., 2015), visual (Larderet et al., 2017), and olfactory (Berck et al., 2016) systems.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Synaptic-resolution electron microscopy reconstructions from Drosophila sensory systems have found relatively low intra-animal variation in number of synaptic contacts between bilaterally repeated neurons in the mechanosensatory, visual, and olfactory systems.
source: However, synaptic-resolution electron microscopy (EM) reconstructions from Drosophila sensory systems have found relatively low intra-animal variation in number of synaptic contacts between columnarly repeated neurons in the adult visual system (Takemura et al., 2015) or bilaterally repeated neurons in the mechanosensatory (Ohyama et al., 2015), visual (Larderet et al., 2017), and olfactory (Berck et al., 2016) systems.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Almost no new functional neurons are added to the larval nervous system between hatching and pupariation.
source: Despite considerable growth in body size between hatching and pupariation, almost no new functional neurons are added to the larval nervous system (Truman and Bate, 1988) and behavior remains largely unchanged (Almeida-Carvalho et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Behavior remains largely unchanged between hatching and pupariation in Drosophila larvae.
source: Despite considerable growth in body size between hatching and pupariation, almost no new functional neurons are added to the larval nervous system (Truman and Bate, 1988) and behavior remains largely unchanged (Almeida-Carvalho et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Central neurons become larger during larval development.
source: Nonetheless, electrophysiological and light microscopy analysis has shown that central neurons become larger (Zwart et al., 2013) and have more synapses both in total (Zwart et al., 2013) and in specific connections (Couton et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Central neurons have more synapses both in total and in specific connections during larval development.
source: Nonetheless, electrophysiological and light microscopy analysis has shown that central neurons become larger (Zwart et al., 2013) and have more synapses both in total (Zwart et al., 2013) and in specific connections (Couton et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Nociceptive stimuli are detected by the three multidendritic class IV sensory neurons (mdIVs) in each hemisegment.
source: Nociceptive stimuli are detected by the three multidendritic class IV sensory neurons (mdIVs) (Hwang et al., 2007) in each hemisegment, with dendrites that tile the body wall (Figure 1A) (Grueber et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: mdIV dendrites tile the body wall.
source: Nociceptive stimuli are detected by the three multidendritic class IV sensory neurons (mdIVs) (Hwang et al., 2007) in each hemisegment, with dendrites that tile the body wall (Figure 1A) (Grueber et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The mdIV terminals in abdominal segment A1 of an early first instar larva EM volume were previously reconstructed.
source: The mdIV terminals in abdominal segment A1 of an early first instar larva EM volume (L1v) were previously reconstructed (Ohyama et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: A new serial section transmission EM volume of a late third instar larva (L3v) was generated spanning several abdominal segments of the ventral nerve cord.
source: We generated a new serial section transmission EM volume of a late third instar larva (L3v) spanning several abdominal segments of the ventral nerve cord (VNC) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Describes the experimental data generation.

claim: The six mdIV terminals (three per hemisegment) in abdominal segment A3 were manually reconstructed in the L3v.
source: In the L3v, we manually reconstructed the six mdIV terminals (three per hemisegment) in abdominal segment A3 (Figure 1B,C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) using the web-based tool CATMAID (Saalfeld et al., 2009; Schneider-Mizell et al., 2016).
evidence: Describes the reconstruction methodology.

claim: Neurons were reconstructed as skeletons, expressing the 3D topology of neuronal arbors, but not their diameter or volume.
source: In all cases, we reconstructed neurons as skeletons, expressing the 3D topology of neuronal arbors, but not their diameter or volume.
evidence: Describes the reconstruction methodology.

claim: The identity of each mdIV terminal was determined based on stereotyped morphological features such as antero-posterior projections, midline crossing, and nerve bundle.
source: The identity of each mdIV terminal was determined based on stereotyped morphological features such as antero-posterior projections, midline crossing, and nerve bundle (Figure 1B,C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2) (Merritt and Whitington, 1995; Grueber et al., 2007; Ohyama et al., 2015).
evidence: Describes the identification methodology with citations.

claim: The morphology of mdIV axon terminals remained similar across larval stages, with growth in overall size but no change in branching patterns.
source: The morphology of mdIV axon terminals remained similar across larval stages, with growth in overall size but no change in branching patterns (Figure 1B–D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data and figures showing morphology.

claim: The number of synaptic outputs increased by a factor of 4.7, from a mean of 185 synapses per terminal to 872 synapses per terminal.
source: However, the number of synaptic outputs increased by a factor of 4.7, from a mean of 185 synapses per terminal to 872 synapses per terminal (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: Quantitative finding from the data.

claim: Insect synapses are polyadic, with multiple post-synaptic targets per pre-synaptic site.
source: Insect synapses are polyadic, with multiple post-synaptic targets per pre-synaptic site (Figure 1G), thus this increase could arise from either changes in the number of distinct pre-synaptic sites or the number of targets per pre-synaptic site.
evidence: General knowledge about insect synapses with reference to figure.

claim: There is no significant difference between the distribution of number of post-synaptic targets for mdIV pre-synaptic sites in the L1v compared to the L3v.
source: We found no significant difference between the distribution of number of post-synaptic targets for mdIV pre-synaptic sites in the L1v compared to the L3v (Figure 1H), suggesting the structure of individual polyadic synapses remains unchanged.
evidence: Statistical finding from the data.

claim: The structure of individual polyadic synapses remains unchanged across larval stages.
source: We found no significant difference between the distribution of number of post-synaptic targets for mdIV pre-synaptic sites in the L1v compared to the L3v (Figure 1H), suggesting the structure of individual polyadic synapses remains unchanged.
evidence: Inference from the statistical finding.

claim: There are 13 distinct cell types stereotypically connected to mdIV terminals.
source: We found that there are 13 distinct cell types stereotypically connected to mdIV terminals (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Finding from comprehensive reconstruction.

claim: Five types of mdIV-connected neurons were local neurons (LNs), with dendrites covering 1–2 segments.
source: Five types were local neurons (LNs), with dendrites covering 1–2 segments (Figure 2B); three were regional, with dendrites covering 3–5 segments; four were ascending neurons projecting across the entire VNC; and one was a descending neuron with an axon that projected along the whole VNC (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Classification based on morphological data.

claim: Three types of mdIV-connected neurons were regional, with dendrites covering 3–5 segments.
source: Five types were local neurons (LNs), with dendrites covering 1–2 segments (Figure 2B); three were regional, with dendrites covering 3–5 segments; four were ascending neurons projecting across the entire VNC; and one was a descending neuron with an axon that projected along the whole VNC (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Classification based on morphological data.

claim: Four types of mdIV-connected neurons were ascending neurons projecting across the entire VNC.
source: Five types were local neurons (LNs), with dendrites covering 1–2 segments (Figure 2B); three were regional, with dendrites covering 3–5 segments; four were ascending neurons projecting across the entire VNC; and one was a descending neuron with an axon that projected along the whole VNC (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Classification based on morphological data.

claim: One type of mdIV-connected neuron was a descending neuron with an axon that projected along the whole VNC.
source: Five types were local neurons (LNs), with dendrites covering 1–2 segments (Figure 2B); three were regional, with dendrites covering 3–5 segments; four were ascending neurons projecting across the entire VNC; and one was a descending neuron with an axon that projected along the whole VNC (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Classification based on morphological data.

claim: One cell type (A02n) was comprised of two indistinguishable cells per hemisegment, making a total of twelve LNs cells per segment.
source: One cell type (A02n) was comprised of two indistinguishable cells per hemisegment, unusual for the larva, making a total of twelve LNs cells per segment.
evidence: Finding from reconstruction data.

claim: Two LNs, A09a and A09c, have been the focus of previous work under the names 'Basin-2' and 'Basin-4'.
source: Note that two LNs, A09a and A09c, have been the focus of previous work under the names 'Basin-2' and 'Basin-4' (Ohyama et al., 2015; Jovanic et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Second-order nociceptive interneurons formed a sparse network, without the densely connected local interneurons found in other early processing of other Drosophila sensory modalities like olfaction or mechanosensation.
source: Second-order nociceptive interneurons formed a sparse network (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C), without the densely connected local interneurons found in other early processing of other Drosophila sensory modalities like olfaction (Berck et al., 2016; Liu and Wilson, 2013) or mechanosensation (Jovanic et al., 2016; Tuthill and Wilson, 2016).
evidence: Comparison with other systems supported by citations.

claim: All twelve third instar LNs were reconstructed in the L3v.
source: To measure how second-order nociceptive interneurons change across larval growth, we reconstructed all twelve third instar LNs in the L3v (Figure 2C).
evidence: Describes the reconstruction work.

claim: Each LN was morphologically identifiable, despite increases in size, arbor complexity, and synaptic count.
source: Each LN was morphologically identifiable, despite increases in size, arbor complexity, and synaptic count (Figure 2B,D).
evidence: Finding from morphological analysis.

claim: For every LN, the spatial segregation of synaptic input and synaptic output made it possible to split neuronal arbors into a separate dendritic domain and axonal domain.
source: For every LN, the spatial segregation of synaptic input and synaptic output made it possible to split neuronal arbors into a separate dendritic domain and axonal domain (Figure 2E).
evidence: Methodological finding from the data.

claim: Only those LN types that exhibited dendritic outputs in the L1v also did so in the L3v.
source: Only those LN types that exhibited dendritic outputs in the L1v also did so in the L3v (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Finding about consistency of dendritic outputs.

claim: For each LN the broad pattern of segregation between synaptic inputs and outputs was preserved over postembryonic development.
source: For each LN the broad pattern of segregation between synaptic inputs and outputs, which indicates the degree of local dendritic output and axonal pre-synaptic input, was preserved over postembryonic development (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: Finding about preservation of segregation patterns.

claim: Every LN in the L3v received synaptic input from mdIVs.
source: Every LN in the L3v received synaptic input from mdIVs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: Finding from connectivity analysis.

claim: LNs do not receive synaptic input equally from all mdIV subtypes.
source: LNs do not receive synaptic input equally from all mdIV subtypes.
evidence: General observation from connectivity data.

claim: The normalized synaptic input into each LN from each mdIV axon was highly structured in both L1v and L3v data.
source: The normalized synaptic input into each LN from each mdIV axon was highly structured in both L1v and L3v data (Figure 3D).
evidence: Finding from connectivity analysis.

claim: For each mdIV type and LN type, the average normalized synaptic input was significantly correlated between L1v and L3v.
source: For each mdIV type and LN type, the average normalized synaptic input was significantly correlated between L1v and L3v (Figure 3E).
evidence: Statistical finding from the data.

claim: The variability between left and right cells of the same type was significantly lower in the L3v than the L1v.
source: Moreover, the variability between left and right cells of the same type was significantly lower in the L3v than the L1v (Figure 3F).
evidence: Statistical finding from the data.

claim: There is effectively a target value for the normalized synaptic input for each connection and this value is achieved more precisely as the nervous system develops postembryonically.
source: These observations suggest that there is, effectively, a target value for the normalized synaptic input for each connection and this value is achieved more precisely as the nervous system develops postembryonically.
evidence: Inference from the correlation and variability findings.

claim: Each segment of the body wall is spanned by six mdIVs whose dendritic fields divide the left and right sides into dorsal, lateral, and ventral thirds.
source: Each segment of the body wall is spanned by six mdIVs whose dendritic fields divide the left and right sides into dorsal, lateral, and ventral thirds (Figure 3G) (Grueber et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: LN orientations span the body wall, and the orientation of LNs are conserved across development.
source: We found that LN orientations span the body wall, and the orientation of LNs are conserved across development.
evidence: Finding from orientation analysis.

claim: LN inputs are arranged so that a nociceptive stimulus smaller than a single mdIV's dendrite is likely to drive different populations of LNs based on its exact location.
source: Further, LN inputs are arranged so that a nociceptive stimulus smaller than a single mdIV's dendrite, for example a wasp ovipositor (Robertson et al., 2013), is likely to drive different populations of LNs based on its exact location, with the smallest difference being between left and right ventral regions (Figure 3D).
evidence: Inference from the connectivity pattern with citation.

claim: Only LNs with similar input orientations synaptically connect to one another.
source: Interestingly, only LNs with similar input orientations synaptically connect to one another (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting that convergent feed-forward motifs are specifically present within sets of neurons likely to be driven at the same time.
evidence: Finding from connectivity analysis.

claim: Conservation of synaptic input through larval development preserves the topographical structure of the nociceptive circuit, both in sensory input and interactions between interneurons.
source: Conservation of synaptic input through larval development thus preserves the topographical structure of the nociceptive circuit, both in sensory input and interactions between interneurons.
evidence: Summary inference from the findings.

claim: Filling fraction ranged from 0.01 to 0.47 in both the L1v and L3v.
source: In both the L1v and L3v, filling fraction ranged from 0.01 to 0.47, indicating that some connections from mdIV types to LNs were realized much more often than others.
evidence: Quantitative finding from the data.

claim: Filling fraction correlated strongly with the overall count of synapses in a connection.
source: Filling fraction correlated strongly with the overall count of synapses in a connection, suggesting that numerically strong connections are produced through high connection probability, not only increased potential synapse counts (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: Statistical finding from the data.

claim: Numerically strong connections are produced through high connection probability, not only increased potential synapse counts.
source: Filling fraction correlated strongly with the overall count of synapses in a connection, suggesting that numerically strong connections are produced through high connection probability, not only increased potential synapse counts (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: Inference from the correlation finding.

claim: Filling fraction was significantly correlated between the L1v and L3v.
source: Moreover, filling fraction was significantly correlated between the L1v and L3v (Figure 4E), suggesting that the local propensity to form stable synapses with a nearby cell type is preserved across development.
evidence: Statistical finding from the data.

claim: The local propensity to form stable synapses with a nearby cell type is preserved across development.
source: Moreover, filling fraction was significantly correlated between the L1v and L3v (Figure 4E), suggesting that the local propensity to form stable synapses with a nearby cell type is preserved across development.
evidence: Inference from the correlation finding.

claim: Most synaptic input onto a neuron is located on 'twigs', spine-like microtubule-free terminal branches hosting a small number of synapses.
source: Most synaptic input onto a neuron is located on 'twigs', spine-like microtubule-free terminal branches hosting a small number of synapses, in contrast to the microtubule-containing 'backbone' that spans the soma and all of the main branches of a neuron (Leiss et al., 2009; Schneider-Mizell et al., 2016) (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Both the fraction of dendritic cable comprised of twigs and the fraction of dendritic input synapses onto twigs increased significantly.
source: Both the fraction of dendritic cable comprised of twigs (Figure 5E,F) and the fraction of dendritic input synapses onto twigs (Figure 5G,H) increased significantly, suggesting that twigs become even more central to dendritic input.
evidence: Statistical finding from the data.

claim: Twigs become even more central to dendritic input during development.
source: Both the fraction of dendritic cable comprised of twigs (Figure 5E,F) and the fraction of dendritic input synapses onto twigs (Figure 5G,H) increased significantly, suggesting that twigs become even more central to dendritic input.
evidence: Inference from the statistical findings.

claim: The fraction of dendritic cable that is last or next-to-last (Strahler order 1 or 2) order is similar not only across development, but also across cell types.
source: We found that the fraction of dendritic cable that is last or next-to-last (Strahler order 1 or 2) order is similar not only across development, but also across cell types (Figure 5K).
evidence: Finding from Strahler order analysis.

claim: Neurons grow their dendrites by both increasing the number of twigs, while also modestly increasing the length of the backbone neurites from which they sprout.
source: This suggests that in the larva, neurons grow their dendrites by both increasing the number of twigs, while also modestly increasing the length of the backbone neurites from which they sprout.
evidence: Inference from the Strahler order and twig findings.

claim: Typical dendritic twigs in both the L1v and L3v are small.
source: Typical dendritic twigs in both the L1v and L3v are small. They were short in both total length and maximum depth from twig root, had few branch points, and few post-synaptic sites (Figure 6A).
evidence: Finding from twig property analysis.

claim: Twigs in the L3v were slightly longer than their L1v counterparts and had significantly more branch points.
source: However, twigs in the L3v were slightly longer than their L1v counterparts and had significantly more branch points (Figure 6A).
evidence: Statistical finding from the data.

claim: The anatomical and numerical redundancy of synapses on LN dendrites resulted in connections that would be detectable with at least 25% of the actual number of synapses, even if twigs were missed at the same rate (12%) as observed in previous work with the same reconstruction method.
source: The anatomical and numerical redundancy of synapses on LN dendrites resulted in connections that would be detectable with at least 25% of the actual number of synapses, even if twigs were missed at the same rate (12%) as observed in previous work with the same reconstruction method (Figure 6E).
evidence: Finding from simulation analysis with reference to prior work.

claim: Numerically strong connections in the L3v were particularly robust, and would still be detectable with a 50% false negative rate.
source: Numerically strong connections in the L3v were particularly robust, and would still be detectable with a 50% false negative rate (Figure 6E).
evidence: Finding from simulation analysis.

claim: For large neurons, a strategy of incomplete sampling could quickly identify numerically strong synaptic partners at the cost of precise measurement of synaptic count.
source: For large neurons, a strategy of incomplete sampling could thus quickly identify numerically strong synaptic partners at the cost of precise measurement of synaptic count.
evidence: Inference from the robustness findings.

claim: Neuronal arbor morphology changes across postembryonic development while circuit connectivity properties remain largely unchanged.
source: We have shown how in Drosophila neuronal arbor morphology changes across postembryonic development while circuit connectivity properties remain largely unchanged.
evidence: Summary of main findings.

claim: Numerically strong connectivity in the L1v predicted the presence of functional connectivity in third instar larvae tested experimentally.
source: Our findings establish a quantitative foundation for the previous observation that numerically strong connectivity in the L1v predicted the presence of functional connectivity in third instar larvae tested experimentally (Ohyama et al., 2015; Zwart et al., 2016; Fushiki et al., 2016; Heckscher et al., 2015; Jovanic et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In all neurons measured, the basic anatomical elements of connectivity — polyadic synapses and small post-synaptic twigs — remained similar, while neurons grew five-fold in total synaptic input and cable length.
source: In all neurons measured, the basic anatomical elements of connectivity — polyadic synapses and small post-synaptic twigs — remained similar, while neurons grew five-fold in total synaptic input and cable length.
evidence: Summary of findings.

claim: Although cell types ranged considerably in size at any given time point, the fold-increase in total cable length and synapse count was nearly constant across cell types.
source: Interestingly, although cell types ranged considerably in size at any given time point, the fold-increase in total cable length and synapse count was nearly constant across cell types.
evidence: Summary of findings.

claim: The sensory connections focused on here are excitatory.
source: We note that the sensory connections we focused on here are excitatory (Ohyama et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The tight control of normalized synaptic input is likely to be in the service of circuit function.
source: The tight control of normalized synaptic input is likely to be in the service of circuit function.
evidence: Interpretation of the findings.

claim: As neurons grow, there is a consistent compensatory growth in synaptic inputs from sensory neurons.
source: Our data suggest that, as neurons grow, there is a consistent compensatory growth in synaptic inputs from sensory neurons.
evidence: Interpretation of the findings.

claim: Central neurons adapt structurally to compensate for increasing volume with concurrent increases in excitatory synaptic currents by adding synaptic contacts, as seen at the neuromuscular junction.
source: This observation suggests that central neurons adapt structurally to compensate for increasing volume with concurrent increases in excitatory synaptic currents by adding synaptic contacts, as seen at the neuromuscular junction (Rasse et al., 2005).
evidence: Interpretation with citation to prior work.

claim: In visual system interneurons in the adult fly, dendritic geometry and membrane properties work together so that, near the spike initiation zone, the functional weight of a synaptic input does not depend strongly on its location on the dendrite.
source: In visual system interneurons in the adult fly, dendritic geometry and membrane properties work together so that, near the spike initiation zone, the functional weight of a synaptic input does not depend strongly on its location on the dendrite (Cuntz et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Simulations based on adult Drosophila olfactory projection neurons reconstructed from EM found that the functional responses were simply proportional to the number of synapses activated, even after shuffling input locations.
source: Similarly, simulations based on adult Drosophila olfactory projection neurons reconstructed from EM found that the functional responses were simply proportional to the number of synapses activated, even after shuffling input locations (Tobin et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Linear dendritic integration of excitatory input may be common, at least in early sensory processing.
source: Taken together, this suggests linear dendritic integration of excitatory input may be common, at least in early sensory processing.
evidence: Inference from cited prior work.

claim: Linear integration would imply that the relative functional weight of each mdIV type is preserved across development.
source: In our data, each mdIV input into LNs typically increased by a common factor, irrespective of specific pre-synaptic cell type. Linear integration would thus imply that the relative functional weight of each mdIV type is preserved across development.
evidence: Inference from the data and linear integration assumption.

claim: The same developmental rules that allow neurons to maintain circuit function as the body grows would also be well-suited to handle natural variability, for example from reduced growth due to food restriction.
source: The same developmental rules that allow neurons to maintain circuit function as the body grows would also be well-suited to handle natural variability, for example from reduced growth due to food restriction (Mirth and Riddiford, 2007).
evidence: Speculation with citation.

claim: The use of consistent homeostatic rules for cell type-specific connectivity and integration could allow circuits to remain functionally or computationally similar over large evolutionary changes in neuron size.
source: Indeed, it is possible that the use of consistent homeostatic rules for cell type-specific connectivity and integration could allow circuits to remain functionally or computationally similar over large evolutionary changes in neuron size.
evidence: Speculation about evolutionary implications.

claim: Calliphora and Drosophila visual system neurons differ in scale by a factor of four in each spatial dimension but have retained similar electrotonic structures.
